title: Prayer, remembrance, and God as the righteous one's only strength
english: The words of supplication are also spoken in songs. But since supplication must be offered with thanksgiving, the song is placed before the prayer. For no one who has been ungrateful for what came before is strong in asking for what is to come. And the request seeks divine remembrance from God. For if I were in remembrance with you, the psalmist says, I would not be going about in gloom and being oppressed by the unjust. It is clear that forgetfulness does not touch the divine nature, since forgetfulness is a change in memory, and the divine is unchangeable. For this reason he also asks, “Why have you forgotten me?” No one says “Why?” about an involuntary experience of forgetfulness; rather, it presents voluntary forgetfulness as neglect of one unworthy of God’s care.

This psalm is inseparable from the previous one, not divided even by a title, and it holds to the same power of the return to God. It adds also the guidance through the light that shone forth, which says, “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who follows me may not remain in darkness” (John 12:46) (Ps 42:1). By this shining it prepares comfort for the one who grieves, just as the psalm before it made comfort for sorrows through the expectation of things to come. Since, then, the portion of the righteous is attacked both nation by nation and man by man, and they cannot obtain what they deserve unless they receive the heavenly judge and advocate—as if the case against their adversaries were a concern to him who judges all justly—he calls upon him, since he judges not from hearsay but brings forth what is just from knowledge. For this reason he asks for escape both from the nation and from the unjust man.

The psalmist says this as one who has nothing else for strength, and he obtains God—as it is also said, “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Psalm 17:2 (18:1)) (Ps 42:2a). Then he speaks here also about those who oppose him.

If strength comes from God, it is reasonable that not being strengthened is a rejection from God, most grievous to the one who puts forward this help alone. The “why” is not as if God does something without cause or in vain—for this happens for our contest—but as if the contest ought to have an end through mercy, and comfort ought to be given to those who mourn by the one who comforts those who mourn (Ps 42:2). For it makes no sense that God would overlook the righteous. Therefore, seeking what comes from God, he says “why” as if to say: It is fitting for you to take hold of your own and not to permit pleasure to your adversaries (Ps 42:4c). Why then is what is yours not accomplished, but what comes from us abounds? As it is also said, “How long, Lord, will you forget me to the end?” (Psalm 12:2 (13:1)) and “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to destruction?” (Ps 42:5) (Psalm 29:10 (30:9)). For even if affliction is necessary for some time, it is not forever; and even if we are justly afflicted on our own account, we ought at least to obtain help according to God’s mercy, so that discipline may give back a peaceful fruit through God’s love for humanity to those who have been trained by it (Ps 42:5). But in the case of the Lord, the “why have you forsaken me” is said in a complete sense, since what concerns him is not worthy of forsaking. Therefore the appearance of heavenly help is swift for the suffering body, because of that which concerns us.
He has shown the brightness by the addition of the lyre, and the love in the address repeated twice.

This is the reminder of comfort. For even if we are weighed down by present things, he says, let us give thanks for the things to come, and already by expectation let the sorrow depart, as we await God, the salvation of the person who looks to him (Ps 43:5).
You, he says, we have as king—God, who provides for the salvation of our people—and we know that you will accomplish this, and we take courage in your will (Ps 43:6).
You, he says, we have as a horn to ward off all enemies, and your name upon us will make those who rise up against us and hope to overpower us a thing to be trampled (Ps 43:6; Ps 43:7).

For I do not prepare myself, he says, with bow and spear (Ps 43:7). Therefore I do not trust in weapons, since these did not suffice even for our fathers, nor was the success accomplished according to their strength, but the work is beyond all human preparation (Ps 43:8).
He says the earlier teachings correspond to the later events. We have been taught that our salvation from adversaries has always come from you, and we have seen their power turned to shame.

For this reason, he says, we boast altogether in you through all time, and we offer thanks to your name by which we are saved—as it is also said through Ezekiel: “It is not for your sake that I act, O house of Israel [the printed text reads νῖκος, 'victory', for οἶκος, 'house'], but for the sake of my name” (Ezekiel 36:22) (Ps 43:9; Ps 43:10.11).

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting verse by verse on Psalms 41-43, explaining how the psalmist's words teach prayer, remembrance before God, and trust in God alone as king and defender.

title: Israel's present shame proves God alone gives victory
english: But these hopes, he says, are firm and unshakable, and we will not abandon them because of what has happened. Yet what has happened now is the opposite of them. For we have been left behind by you, he says, having been thrust away, and you are not present with our armies. The shame that then seized the battles has come around upon us, and we have been diminished before those whom we formerly mastered, and we have been plundered by those whom we plundered. For in this it has been shown all the more by God that the strength belonged to Israel, since when they are abandoned they are defeated—just as for man, being abandoned became the occasion of death, showing that resurrection comes from God alone and in no other way (Ps 43:12).

We have been gripped by cowardice, he says, a cowardice unable to defend us against those who devour us like sheep. This is the cowardice that Moses also threatened would seize them for their transgressions, because the sound of a driven leaf would pursue them. And we have become captives, he says, and we have been scattered among the nations—we who were formerly brought out from the nations and possessed the holy land. This is a dissolution of honor, just as for man the dissolution of his formation is the saying, “Earth you are, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). So also Isaiah says about the people: “We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us and your mercy was not called upon us” (Isaiah 63:19) (Ps 43:13a).

Freely they were sold, as Isaiah also says. And he says they were sold for their sins, just as Paul says about man: “I am fleshly, sold under sin” (Romans 7:14). The sale is the alienation and the coming to be under human masters instead of God. This is what he also threatened Jeroboam and the people with him through Shemaiah the prophet: that they would become slaves to the Egyptian king Shishak, and they would know the slavery of God and the slavery of the kings of the earth (Ps 43:15).

For such a thing is a parable—that they are remembered in the curses. Just as Jeremiah says against the false prophets: “They will take up a curse against him in the exile, O Judah, in Babylon, saying, ‘May the Lord do to you as he did to Zedekiah and as to Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in fire because of the lawlessness they committed in Israel’” . Grant these things now, and most justly: they are devoured like sheep, when they led Christ like a sheep to slaughter; they are sold to the nations, just as they bought the Lord, betrayed for silver and in some way handed over to death; they are mocked, just as they made mockery and shaking of heads at the crucified Lord (Ps 43:18-21).

This alone remains to Israel as a hope for the recall of those who are left, which the prophecy foreseeing says: that they did not turn aside to the customs of the Greeks according to the idolatry they had agreed upon, nor did they swerve from the path of piety toward the one God that had been commanded them, even though they were so humbled and exiled and placed under the authority of those who kill. This was preserved especially by those around Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, who endured fire rather than accept worship of idols. And indeed, this is not present as something pious among the remaining Jews at the present time. For while they do not entirely abandon the practice of not going to idols or the Greek sickness of incantations, their impiety toward Christ is shown to be most harmful in this way: because, not worshiping idols as before, they are enslaved as never before (Ps 44:2).

Having mentioned the Israelite evils before this and having left behind the grace that releases from evils—a grace beginning from the nations but also taking up no small portion of those from Israel, for many from the Jews have believed—he makes a kind of prelude of the initiation concerning these things. He announces a good word about the coming of the king, who oversees the works of the righteous for his contemplation, and which are brought up by them as a kind of hearing for him, and who gives to them the divine fulfillment. For he has come as the fulfiller of what is not truly fulfilled among human beings, lawful by divine purity and by the sanctifying participation that comes from him. And he indicates that he will say many things quickly, comparing the tongue that declares these things to the pen of a very swift scribe.

Isaiah foresees his outward appearance failing compared to the sons of men, prophesying his dishonor according to the flesh (Ps 44:3ab). But David interprets the divine beauty, which is also made clear in Isaiah through the words that the king will be seen with glory.

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 43 (44), where Israel laments that God has rejected them in battle despite their faithfulness, and he reads this as a proof that strength comes only from God.

title: The anointing of Christ and the bride's beauty
english: This points to the ineffable glory and beauty of the invisible one, and he foretells the manifestation of that beauty through words and deeds, saying that grace has been poured out on his lips, just as the Gospels also make clear that everyone marveled at the words of grace that came from his mouth (cf (Ps 44:8). Luke 4:22).

So, he says, as in a pure vessel the divine ointment has been anointed upon him, joined by nature and not by participation because of kinship—not given by grace as it is also to your partakers. And he addresses Christ as God, and says that the one who anoints him is his God, not abolishing the human constitution and the Word's relation to the flesh, according to which there is also an anointing of the Spirit, since the flesh was sanctified beforehand and sanctified again through the Spirit who was present from the beginning and came again. For from the beginning, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you' (Luke 1:35); and again, 'Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power' (Acts 10:38). But if it were not said that the Spirit is joined to him as to natural beauty by kinship, then this anointing would be spoken of as something earned through practice. And where can anyone point to such practice? What labor of learning was there in Christ, so that holiness might be a recompense for labors? Would the Spirit of wisdom come upon him through diligent learning, and would the steadfast and powerful Spirit be sealed upon him through battle against pleasures? It is clear, then, that the anointing is spoken of as something that follows by nature and not as something given in return for labor, and the Spirit was not given to him as a wage to a human being—though even this would be possible, for God gives the Spirit by grace and not as a wage—but as to one who is at once God and man, what was his own was manifested from him and toward him, just as we humans, offering what is our own to God, say, 'Therefore I will confess you among the nations, O Lord' (Psalm 17:50 (18:49)).

By saying 'partakers,' he also showed the reason for the anointing: so that the anointing by participation might go forward, for this reason the anointing by participation also came. For as far as the Lord himself was concerned, there was no need of anointing, since he was holy by nature and became holy, and placed holiness as something innate in his body, and by this brought the human form to maturity. But since this was not in us, nor was it possible among human beings to be holy by nature, but there is need of gift and heavenly grace, for this reason the Spirit came upon Christ, so that he might show us as led from him to participation in the Spirit through kinship according to the body (Ps 44:12a).

The departure of the nations from evil things makes the bride beautiful and desirable to the king. For this is our beauty, and by this we are adorned, and by this we are made close to God, and so greatly do we become sought after by God that he speaks according to his desire, the kind of things a lover would say about the beauty of his beloved.

The bride is near the king, and virgins are near her and follow her, and through her they are made close to the king, like attendants accompanying a bride, young maidens (Ps 44:15). To her, according to the Song of Solomon, the synagogues of the Jews would most fittingly be second and following, according to 'The first will be last and the last first' (Matthew 20:16), and 'The proselyte among you will rise above you as head, and you will be as the tail' (Deuteronomy 28:43-44). For those who long ago became proselytes of the law in order to be made close to God now themselves lead the assembly that draws near to God, and this is clear from what follows.

For this queen stands beside Christ and enters with him into his holy temple, and she gives the inheritance of the world and the kingdom promised to Abraham to those descended from him according to bodily lineage, with the king willing it and the queen consenting (Ps 44:16b). Therefore those young maidens whom he said were fathers he now calls sons, since they have received the rank of sons and being deemed worthy of inheritance from their mother as sons (Ps 45:6).

He says the city will be indestructible, so that God will be in it, when the present night ceases at early dawn. For it is night as long as the darkness has not been entirely removed nor every authority and power abolished, but they still stir up warlike attempts against the righteous (Ps 44:25).

Not even when you were handed over to the nations, he says, abandoned by God, were you handed over in vain, but so that you might know the power of God, who acquired all the nations for your reproof, and who acquired every land instead of one land under his own worship, because by the same transgression, according to the apostle, salvation has come to the nations to provoke Israel to jealousy  (Ps 46).
